{{Short description|In mathematics, a type of conformal map}}
{{more footnotes|date=May 2017}}
[[File:joukowsky transform.svg|thumb|right|350px|Example of a Joukowsky transform. The circle above is transformed into the Joukowsky airfoil below.]]

In [[applied mathematics]], the '''Joukowsky transform''' (sometimes transliterated ''Joukovsky'', ''Joukowski'' or ''Zhukovsky'') is a [[conformal map]] historically used to understand some principles of [[airfoil]] design. It is named after [[Nikolay Yegorovich Zhukovsky|Nikolai Zhukovsky]], who published it in 1910.<ref>{{cite journal | last=Joukowsky | first=N. E. | authorlink=Nikolay Yegorovich Zhukovsky | title=Über die Konturen der Tragflächen der Drachenflieger | journal=Zeitschrift für Flugtechnik und Motorluftschiffahrt | year=1910 | volume=1 | pages=281–284 and (1912) '''3''': 81–86 |lang=de}}</ref>

The transform and its right-inverse are

: <math>z = \zeta + \frac{1}{\zeta},\qquad \zeta=\tfrac12z \pm\sqrt{\bigl(\tfrac12z\bigr)^2-1} = \frac1{\tfrac12z\mp\sqrt{\bigl(\tfrac12z\bigr)^2-1}},</math>

where <math>z = x + iy</math> is a [[complex number|complex variable]] in the new space and <math>\zeta = \chi + i \eta</math> is a complex variable in the original space.
The right-inverse is not a global left-inverse because <math>\zeta\mapsto z</math> is 2-to-1; but a local left-inverse is always one of the right-inverse branches.

In [[aerodynamics]], the transform is used to solve for the two-dimensional [[potential flow]] around a class of airfoils known as Joukowsky airfoils.  A '''Joukowsky airfoil''' is generated in the [[complex plane]] (<math>z</math>-plane) by applying the Joukowsky transform to a circle in the <math>\zeta</math>-plane.  The coordinates of the centre of the circle are variables, and varying them modifies the shape of the resulting airfoil.  The circle encloses the point <math>\zeta = -1</math> (where the derivative is zero) and intersects the point <math>\zeta = 1.</math> This can be achieved for any allowable centre position <math>\mu_x + i\mu_y</math> by varying the radius of the circle.

Joukowsky airfoils have a [[cusp (singularity)|cusp]] at their [[trailing edge]]. A closely related conformal mapping, the [[#Kármán–Trefftz transform|Kármán–Trefftz transform]], generates the broader class of Kármán–Trefftz airfoils by controlling the trailing edge angle. When a trailing edge angle of zero is specified, the Kármán–Trefftz transform reduces to the Joukowsky transform.

==General Joukowsky transform==
The Joukowsky transform of any complex number <math>\zeta</math> to <math>z</math> is as follows:

:<math>\begin{align}
  z &= x + iy = \zeta + \frac{1}{\zeta} \\
    &= \chi + i \eta + \frac{1}{\chi + i\eta} \\[2pt]
    &= \chi + i \eta + \frac{\chi - i\eta}{\chi^2 + \eta^2} \\[2pt]
    &= \chi\left(1 + \frac1{\chi^2 + \eta^2}\right) + i\eta\left(1 - \frac1{\chi^2 + \eta^2}\right).
\end{align}</math>

So the real (<math>x</math>) and imaginary (<math>y</math>) components are:

:<math>\begin{align}
  x &= \chi\left(1 + \frac1{\chi^2 + \eta^2}\right), \\[2pt]
  y &= \eta\left(1 - \frac1{\chi^2 + \eta^2}\right).
\end{align}</math>

===Sample Joukowsky airfoil===
The transformation of all complex numbers on the [[unit circle]] is a special case.

<math display="block">|\zeta| = \sqrt{\chi^2 + \eta^2} = 1,</math>

which gives

<math display="block">\chi^2 + \eta^2 = 1.</math>

So the real component becomes <math display=inline>x = \chi (1 + 1) = 2\chi</math> and the imaginary component becomes <math display=inline>y = \eta (1 - 1) = 0</math>.

Thus the complex unit circle maps to a flat plate on the real-number line from −2 to +2.

Transformations from other circles make a wide range of airfoil shapes.

==Velocity field and circulation for the Joukowsky airfoil==

The solution to [[potential flow around a circular cylinder]] is [[analytic function|analytic]] and well known.  It is the superposition of [[uniform flow]], a [[doublet (potential flow)|doublet]], and a [[vortex]].

The [[complex conjugate]] velocity <math>\widetilde{W} = \widetilde{u}_x - i\widetilde{u}_y,</math> around the circle in the <math>\zeta</math>-plane is
<math display="block">\widetilde{W} = V_\infty e^{-i\alpha} + \frac{i\Gamma}{2\pi(\zeta - \mu)} - \frac{V_\infty R^2 e^{i\alpha}}{(\zeta - \mu)^2}, </math>

where
* <math>\mu = \mu_x + i \mu_y</math> is the complex coordinate of the centre of the circle,
* <math>V_\infty</math> is the [[uniform flow|freestream velocity]] of the fluid,
<math>\alpha</math> is the [[angle of attack]] of the airfoil with respect to the freestream flow,
* <math>R</math> is the radius of the circle, calculated using <math display="inline">R = \sqrt{\left(1 - \mu_x\right)^2 + \mu_y^2}</math>,
* <math>\Gamma</math> is the [[circulation (fluid dynamics)|circulation]], found using the [[Kutta condition]], which reduces in this case to <math display="block">\Gamma = 4\pi V_\infty R\sin\left(\alpha + \sin^{-1}\frac{\mu_y}{R}\right).</math>

The complex velocity <math>W</math> around the airfoil in the <math>z</math>-plane is, according to the rules of conformal mapping and using the Joukowsky transformation,
<math display="block">W = \frac{\widetilde{W}}{\frac{dz}{d\zeta}} = \frac{\widetilde{W}}{1 - \frac{1}{\zeta^2}}.</math>

Here <math>W = u_x - i u_y,</math> with <math>u_x</math> and <math>u_y</math> the velocity components in the <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> directions respectively (<math>z = x + iy,</math> with <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> real-valued). From this velocity, other properties of interest of the flow, such as the [[coefficient of pressure]] and [[lift (force)|lift]] per unit of span can be calculated.

== Kármán–Trefftz transform == <!-- [[Kármán–Trefftz airfoil]] and [[Kármán–Trefftz transform]] redirect here -->
[[File:Karman Trefftz transform.svg|thumb|300px|right|Example of a Kármán–Trefftz transform. The circle above in the {{nowrap|<math>\zeta</math>-plane}} is transformed into the Kármán–Trefftz airfoil below, in the {{nowrap|<math>z</math>-plane}}. The parameters used are: <math>\mu_x = -0.08,</math> <math>\mu_y = +0.08</math> and <math>n = 1.94.</math> Note that the airfoil in the <math>z</math>-plane has been normalised using the [[chord (aircraft)|chord]] length.]]
The '''Kármán–Trefftz transform''' is a conformal map closely related to the Joukowsky transform.  While a Joukowsky airfoil has a cusped trailing edge, a '''Kármán–Trefftz airfoil'''—which is the result of the transform of a circle in the <math>\zeta</math>-plane to the physical <math>z</math>-plane, analogue to the definition of the Joukowsky airfoil—has a non-zero angle at the trailing edge, between the upper and lower airfoil surface.  The Kármán–Trefftz transform therefore requires an additional parameter: the trailing-edge angle <math>\alpha.</math> This transform is<ref name=MT>{{Cite book | first=Louis M. | last=Milne-Thomson | authorlink=L. M. Milne-Thomson | title=Theoretical aerodynamics | url=https://archive.org/details/theoreticalaerod00miln_923 | url-access=limited | edition=4th | publisher=Dover Publ. | year=1973 | isbn=0-486-61980-X | pages=[https://archive.org/details/theoreticalaerod00miln_923/page/n74 128]–131 }}</ref><ref name=JB>{{Cite document | first=J. J. H. | last=Blom | authorlink=J. J. H. Blom | title=Some Characteristic Quantities of Karman-Trefftz Profiles | publisher=NASA Technical Memorandum TM-77013 | year=1981 }}</ref>

{{NumBlk
 |:|<math>z = nb \frac{(\zeta + b)^n + (\zeta - b)^n}{(\zeta + b)^n - (\zeta - b)^n},</math>
 | {{EquationRef|A}}
}}

where <math>b</math> is a real constant that determines the positions where <math>dz/d\zeta = 0</math>, and <math>n</math> is slightly smaller than 2.  The angle <math>\alpha</math> between the [[tangent]]s of the upper and lower airfoil surfaces at the trailing edge is related to <math>n</math> as<ref name=MT/>

: <math>\alpha = 2\pi - n\pi, \quad n = 2 - \frac{\alpha}{\pi}.</math>

The derivative <math>dz/d\zeta</math>, required to compute the velocity field, is

: <math>\frac{dz}{d\zeta} = \frac{4n^2}{\zeta^2 - 1}
 \frac{\left(1 + \frac{1}{\zeta}\right)^n \left(1 - \frac{1}{\zeta}\right)^n}
      {\left[\left(1 + \frac{1}{\zeta}\right)^n - \left(1 - \frac{1}{\zeta}\right)^n \right]^2}.
</math>

===Background===

First, add and subtract 2 from the Joukowsky transform, as given above:

: <math>\begin{align}
  z + 2 &= \zeta + 2 + \frac{1}{\zeta} = \frac{1}{\zeta} (\zeta + 1)^2, \\[3pt]
  z - 2 &= \zeta - 2 + \frac{1}{\zeta} = \frac{1}{\zeta} (\zeta - 1)^2.
\end{align}</math>

Dividing the left and right hand sides gives

: <math>\frac{z - 2}{z + 2} = \left( \frac{\zeta - 1}{\zeta + 1} \right)^2.</math>

The [[right hand side]] contains (as a factor) the simple second-power law from [[potential flow]] theory, applied at the trailing edge near <math>\zeta = +1.</math> From conformal mapping theory, this quadratic map is known to change a half plane in the <math>\zeta</math>-space into potential flow around a semi-infinite straight line. Further, values of the power less than 2 will result in flow around a finite angle. So, by changing the power in the Joukowsky transform to a value slightly less than 2, the result is a finite angle instead of a cusp. Replacing 2 by <math>n</math> in the previous equation gives<ref name=MT/>

: <math>\frac{z - n}{z + n} = \left( \frac{\zeta - 1}{\zeta + 1} \right)^n,</math>

which is the Kármán–Trefftz transform. Solving for <math>z</math> gives it in the form of equation {{EquationNote|A}}.

==Symmetrical Joukowsky airfoils==
In 1943 [[Hsue-shen Tsien]] published a transform of a circle of radius <math>a</math> into a symmetrical airfoil that depends on parameter <math>\epsilon</math> and angle of inclination <math>\alpha</math>:<ref>{{cite journal | first = Hsue-shen |last=Tsien |author-link=Hsue-shen Tsien |year=1943 |title=Symmetrical Joukowsky airfoils in shear flow |journal=Quarterly of Applied Mathematics |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=130–248 |doi=10.1090/qam/8537 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

: <math>z = e^{i\alpha} \left(\zeta - \epsilon + \frac{1}{\zeta - \epsilon} + \frac{2\epsilon^2}{a + \epsilon}\right).</math>

The parameter <math>\epsilon</math> yields a flat plate when zero, and a circle when infinite; thus it corresponds to the thickness of the airfoil. Furthermore the radius of the cylinder <math>a=1+\epsilon</math>.
